parts.title: My lucky number
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
For as long as I can remember, my lucky number has been seven. I was born on the seventh of July, my house is number seven, and I once won a prize in a raffle with ticket number seventy-seven. My friends say that this is just a coincidence, but I am not so sure.

Before every football match, I follow the same routine. I put my left boot on first, I tie the laces twice, and I touch the goalpost before I step onto the pitch. If I forget one of these things, I feel that something bad will happen. Last season I forgot to tie my laces twice and we lost five-nil, though the other team was very good.

My coach does not agree with me. He says that good players make their own luck by training hard. He is probably right, and I do train three times a week. But I still do my routine, because it makes me feel calm.

The funny thing is that I am not the only one. Half of the players in my team have a lucky charm, and one boy never washes his shirt during the season. I try to sit far from him on the bus.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer like the number seven?
options: It appears often in his life
His coach chose it for him
It is the number on his shirt
His mother was born on the seventh
questions.explanation: He was born on the seventh, lives at number seven and won a prize with ticket seventy-seven.

options: He talks to the other team
He asks his team to pray
questions.explanation: He follows the same routine before every match.

questions.prompt: What happened when he forgot to tie his laces twice?
options: He was dropped from the team
questions.explanation: They lost five-nil.

questions.prompt: What does his coach believe?
options: Routines are a waste of time
questions.explanation: He says that good players make their own luck by training hard.

options: The boy never washes his shirt
The boy sings loudly all the time
The boy always talks about luck
questions.explanation: The boy never washes his shirt during the season.

parts.title: Strange beliefs around the world
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Superstitions are found in every country, and many of them are very old. [1] In Britain, for example, people say that walking under a ladder brings bad luck.

Some beliefs are about animals. In many countries, a black cat that crosses your path is a bad sign. [2] But in the United Kingdom, a black cat is thought to bring good luck.

Some are about numbers. In Italy, seventeen is thought to be unlucky. [3] Many hotels in Italy have no room with that number.

Other beliefs are about food. In Japan, you should never stick your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice. [4] It looks like something that is done at a funeral.

Many people laugh at these beliefs. [5] Still, they often do them just in case, because nobody wants to take a risk.
sentences: The reason is that the Roman numerals can be rearranged to mean "I have lived".
Some of them are shared by many countries, but others are only local.
Our grandparents often told us stories of this kind.
Opening an umbrella inside a house is also supposed to bring bad luck.
In Germany, a chimney sweep is considered a sign of good luck.
It is rude, and that is why people avoid it.
They admit that there is no proof that they work.
Sailors, however, consider it a sign of good fortune.

gaps.explanation: Some superstitions are only local, and "in Britain, for example" gives one of them.
Sailors consider the cat a good sign, which leads to the contrast in the United Kingdom.
The reason is about Roman numerals, and the next sentence says hotels have no such room.
It is rude, and the next sentence says it looks like something at a funeral.
They admit there is no proof, and "Still" in the next sentence shows the contrast.

parts.title: The four-leaf clover
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Many people believe that a four-leaf clover brings good luck. A normal clover has three leaves, so a four-leaf clover is quite rare. In fact, there is only [1] four-leaf clover for every ten thousand ordinary ones. People used to think that [2] you found one, you could see fairies. Today, people still collect them and put them inside books. Some even sell them [3] money. When I was small, my grandmother used to take me to the field behind her house. We looked for hours [4] we found a four-leaf clover. I have kept it in a frame ever since. I do not know whether it has really brought me luck, [5] it always reminds me of her. It is a lovely memory, and I think that this is the real reason why people like [6] kind of charm.

gaps.explanation: There is only one four-leaf clover for every ten thousand: the number.
If you found one, you could see fairies: a condition.
Sell them for money: the preposition for price.
Looked for hours until we found one: a limit in time.
Does not know whether it brought luck, but it reminds me of her: contrast.
This kind of charm: a determiner before kind.

parts.title: A talk about strange beliefs
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: nathalie
turns.text: Good afternoon. My name is Bree, and I study the history of beliefs. Today I would like to tell you about a few famous ones and where they come from. First, the number thirteen. Many people are afraid of it, and you can see this in tall buildings. In lots of hotels and offices, there is no thirteenth floor. They go from twelve to fourteen. Some buildings also skip the fourth floor, but that is in other countries. Next, mirrors. We all know the saying that if you break a mirror, you have seven years of bad luck. This idea is very old. It comes from the Romans, who believed that a mirror held part of your soul, and that life renewed itself every seven years. Some books say it was the Greeks, but the number seven is a Roman one. Now, salt. In the past, salt was expensive, so spilling it was a disaster. To stop the bad luck, people threw a pinch of it over the left shoulder, because they thought the devil stood there. Not the right shoulder, that is where the good angel stands. Then, umbrellas. Opening one indoors is unlucky. This belief began in the eighteenth century, when umbrellas had metal parts that could hurt someone in a small room. Some people think it is much older, from ancient Egypt, but the modern story is from the seventeen hundreds. Finally, I think many beliefs began as common sense. Do not walk under a ladder, because something may fall on you. Do not break mirrors, because the glass cuts you. It is not magic at all, just a warning. Of course, some people say it is about religion, but I prefer the practical explanation. Thank you for listening, and now I’m happy to answer your questions.

gaps.explanation: She says she studies the history of beliefs.

gaps.prompt: Many tall buildings leave out the ___ floor
gaps.explanation: In many hotels and offices there is no thirteenth floor; the fourth floor is skipped only in other countries.

gaps.prompt: The saying about a broken mirror comes from the ___
gaps.explanation: It comes from the Romans; some books say the Greeks, but seven is a Roman number.

gaps.prompt: People threw a pinch of ___ over their left shoulder
gaps.explanation: They threw salt over the left shoulder to stop the bad luck.

gaps.prompt: The umbrella belief began in the ___ century
gaps.explanation: It began in the eighteenth century, not in ancient Egypt.
Bree thinks that many beliefs began as common sense, not magic or religion.

parts.title: An interview with a goalkeeper
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Bram, you’re a goalkeeper with many habits. What do you do before a match?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Well, the list is long. People think I eat a banana and an apple, but I have a plain sandwich at twelve. Then I put on my left glove first, always, before the right one. And I don’t phone my father before the game, though he calls me afterwards. The left glove is the rule.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why did you start these habits?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My father didn’t tell me to do them, and I never copied a famous player. It was my first big match, when I was fifteen. I put on the left glove first by accident, and I played the best game of my life. So I did it again the next week, and the next. I’m afraid it became a habit.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What happened when you forgot one?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Once, I put on the right glove first by mistake. I realised on the pitch, and I felt terrible. I played badly, I let in a silly goal, but my team scored three, so we won. I wasn’t sent off and it wasn’t a final, thank goodness. Afterwards I thought it was just a coincidence.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Does the whole team have a ritual?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Yes, and it’s the best part. No matching socks, we’re not a circus, and we don’t sing, nobody can sing. Before every game the players touch an old ball that belonged to our first coach. It’s in a glass box in the changing room. We touch it one by one on the way out.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Do you believe that luck matters more than skill?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s a good question. Luck is part of the game, a ball can hit the post and go in or out. But training is what wins matches. I train six days a week, and I’d say that’s what counts. I wouldn’t say they’re equal, skill is more important.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why is a good friend in the team worth more than any charm?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not money, and not new boots, I’ve had expensive ones that hurt my feet. A good friend, someone who tells you the truth after a bad game, is worth more than all the lucky charms in the world. When I’ve made a mistake, a friend makes me laugh and helps me forget it, and that is better than any glove.

parts.prompt: A friend is going to take an important exam. Talk about the different good-luck presents that you could give and decide which would be the best one.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Why do you think people believe in luck?
Is it silly to follow superstitions? Why or why not?
Would you like to know your future? Why or why not?
